body.text: The sociology of education got off to a flying start in the 1950s and 1960s: against the prevailing assumption that kids got on well or badly at school according to their “ability,” sociology tracked and mapped and demonstrated beyond question that where you got to depended also on where you started. Sociology boosted the demand heard across the Western world for more, and more “equal,” schooling. A major national review of schooling in Australia in the early 1970s was typical in devoting an entire chapter to “equality of opportunity” and in drawing on sociology from Australia, England and Sweden to do it.

By the late 1970s sociology was falling from grace. Policy-makers had found that distributing success more evenly across social groups was harder than it looked; they relegated the struggle for “equality” to ritual incantations and palliatives for the most “disadvantaged.” On the academic left, “arithmetic sociology” was attacked for its distance from real life, its patronising downward gaze, its merely distributional view of equality, and its failure to comprehend the relationship between schooling and social power. I should disclose that I was among those critics.

Half a century later much of the sociology of education is still on about inequality, and still on about it in the same old way. It doesn’t look like it, because sociology now draws on elaborate theories and sophisticated methods, examines gender, racial and other inequalities as well as class and, perhaps driven by growing anger at the accumulation of massive private fortunes, sometimes gazes upward to look at schooling’s role in what it calls the “reproduction of privilege.” And, rather than survey patterns of privilege-distribution from a great height, it sometimes gets up close and personal.

Hence the highly favourable reception accorded to Emma Taylor’s An Elite Education, an “ethnographic” study of a single high-end English boys’ school. Unusually, the ethnographer in this case was a native: her family’s relationship with what she calls “Fortune Park School” extends over three generations; she was a teacher there; and she herself is a product of a school of the Fortune Park kind. To these affordances Taylor added an unusually extensive and extended research process; years as a “participant observer” was combined with interviews, fossicking through school records, “peer-led” focus groups and bumping into members of “the school community” in the normal course of daily life. Thanks to maternity leave and Covid, Taylor’s field work extended over seven years, which meant that she could follow up with some students as they went on to university and then out into employment.

The upshot is admirably lucid, succinct and coherent; it is, as one cover endorsement has it, “beautifully written and engaging.” But it does not — as another endorsement would have it — “force a fundamental rethink of how we talk about merit, success and fairness.” To the contrary. For reasons of both method and theory, An Elite Education works within the ideas of merit, success and fairness as they were understood fifty or sixty years ago.

Taylor set out to discover how Fortune Park “reproduces privilege” — what did it do exactly, to send the offspring of the privileged on their unerring way to becoming privileged themselves? She finds the answer in two fundamentals of life at Fortune Park: first, it is a “home away from home” — its students are, she says, quoting the French reproduction theorist Pierre Bourdieu, “fish in water.” And, second, the teacher–student hierarchy at Fortune Park is “flattened” — there is an ease and informality in relations between teacher and taught that allows and encourages the boys to “practise navigating relationships with those in authority without fear or trepidation.” It is a “forgiving environment” that “absorbs mistakes” in the development of a distinctive mode of bearing and interaction that Taylor calls “audacity.”

Well, yes, and no. Yes, no doubt that is the kind of thing that schools like Fortune Park do, and no doubt “audacity” is particularly important in the English form of class relations, particularly dependent as it seems to be on habits of command and deference.
But no, that’s not all that such schools do; and no, they don’t do it all by themselves.

Fortune Park is a creature of a very particular kind of schooling system, one that allows a very few schools to charge a bomb, thus keeping out all except the already “privileged” as well as furnishing the wherewithal for that home-away-from-home feel. What’s more, the system lets those schools run themselves within a quasi-market and to thereby maintain a constant alertness to the needs, wishes and whims of their clienteles.

And no, the boys aren’t propelled up that “pipeline” to Oxford on pure audacity either, though no doubt it helps when it comes to interviews and the like. Crucially, schools like Fortune Park make sure that their students do very well in a curriculum organised as the kind of competition that suits some very much better than others, and thereby looks fair, but it isn’t.

To her credit, Taylor objects to this unfairness. But note the entailed assumption: everyone should have an equal chance to join the privileged. This is the kind of sociology of education (and sociology of “elites”), almost obsessed as it is with individual trajectories, that has encouraged so many education and social reformers to try to get a rigged system to do what it’s not designed to do and to miss in the process what else is going on.

In its search for the how of “reproduction” — which I should note is not nearly as smooth and certain as the term implies — the ethnology of the school is myopic, even solipsistic, if it doesn’t hook up with the long and wide view of the system within which the school operates.

Just such a view was offered to English sociology nearly seventy years ago when Michael Young published The Rise of the Meritocracy. Young’s argument was that, contra the academic and other attention given to social mobility, “meritocracy” was not a solvent of class that has given individuals the capacity to move hither and yon. It was a new form of class relations thrown up in Britain’s 200-year transition from land-based feudalism to a new industry-based social order.

The consequent demand by those below for “equality” — that is, for full access to the riches of the culture and to the social and political life of the nation — was coopted by the dominant order and turned into “equality of opportunity,” the chance for individuals and families to “improve” themselves. A genuinely democratic impulse was degraded into a much thinner thing, mere egalitarianism (its particularly Australian form: the “equality of manners”). Young further insisted that an apparently fair but actually deeply unfair allocation of social places via schooling, as detected and protested against by the sociologies of education and elites, was intrinsic to the meritocracy, a feature not a bug.

But the meritocracy’s really fundamental business was in legitimating a social system that, in Young’s view, should be seen as unacceptable, not least on account of its exclusion of working-class kids from a genuinely educative schooling, and of the emotional damage done to them in the process of exclusion.

Mainstream sociology of education has failed to consider whether this is a helpful way of understanding things — and whether it should see itself as a part of such a history. It has also failed to consider whether a distributive conception of “equality” might be okay for grown-ups and their relative amounts of wealth, income, status and so on but not okay for the education of children and young people who, by definition cannot be said to “deserve” anything less than a safe, happy and worthwhile twelve years at school.

Of course there are all sorts of dilemmas and difficulties in understanding whether and how two such different ideals can coexist within a single school system and, if so, on what basis — something else a more constructive sociology of education might concern itself with. •
